playground.label: Toy proof-of-work miner (uses input)
playground.code:
import hashlib
prefix = input('Block data: ')
zeros = int(input('Leading zeros required: '))
nonce = 0
while not hashlib.sha256(f'{prefix}-{nonce}'.encode()).hexdigest().startswith('0' * zeros):
    nonce += 1
print(f'nonce {nonce} gives', hashlib.sha256(f'{prefix}-{nonce}'.encode()).hexdigest())

unit.label: Bitcoin in numbers
unit.sub: supplement to chapters 1 and 2: price, supply and mining power since 2009
unit.intro: The owner's dashboard of Bitcoin's price, supply and mining power, from Blockchain.com's public charts (snapshot of 25 September 2026), turned into course material with the chapter pages' tools: explorer, agents, concept map and playground. It makes chapter 1's supply schedule and chapter 2's security by computation visible.

title: Bitcoin in numbers: price, supply and mining power since 2009

nodes.label: Price
nodes.body: The first part of the dashboard follows the market price, where boom-and-bust cycles dominate the history (Blockchain.com, 2026).

nodes.label: Price history
nodes.body: The price history is shown two ways: the full series, and each year's range (Blockchain.com, 2026).

nodes.label: Market price
nodes.body: The chart Market price, USD shows the market price: the average US-dollar price across major exchanges; a logarithmic scale shows the whole history and a linear scale shows recent dollar swings, and the price at its last sample was 86,184.81 dollars (Blockchain.com, 2026).
nodes.example: the average USD price across exchanges
nodes.definition: The average US-dollar price across major exchanges, sampled about every four days; halvings are marked on the chart.

nodes.label: Yearly trading range
nodes.body: In the Yearly trading range chart each year appears as a floating bar from its low to its high with the closing price marked, so a volatile year is a tall bar (Blockchain.com, 2026).
nodes.example: each year's low, high and close
nodes.definition: Floating bars from each year's lowest to highest price, with the closing price marked.

nodes.label: Price change
nodes.body: Change is easier to compare than level when prices span six orders of magnitude (Blockchain.com, 2026).

nodes.label: Year-on-year change
nodes.body: The Year-on-year change chart compares each close with the previous close; bars beyond plus 400 per cent are cut off and labelled (Blockchain.com, 2026).
nodes.definition: Each year's closing price compared with the previous year's close.

nodes.label: Supply
nodes.body: The second part, Minted coins, shows the coins issued against the 21 million cap that chapter 1 describes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Circulation
nodes.body: Circulation is the running total of every block subsidy paid so far (Blockchain.com, 2026).

nodes.label: Circulating supply
nodes.body: The Circulating supply chart grows in steps toward the 21 million ceiling, each step flatter than the last (Blockchain.com, 2026).
nodes.definition: The number of bitcoins issued so far, growing in steps toward the 21 million cap.

nodes.label: Mined vs still to mine
nodes.body: Mined vs still to mine puts it plainly: at the snapshot, 20,087,925 bitcoins had been issued - 95.66 per cent of the 21 million cap - leaving less than a twentieth to be mined over more than a century (Blockchain.com, 2026).
nodes.example: share of the cap already issued
nodes.definition: The issued share of the 21 million cap against what remains to be mined.

nodes.label: Issuance
nodes.body: Yearly issuance falls in steps because the block subsidy halves every 210,000 blocks (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026).

nodes.label: Annual issuance
nodes.body: The chart New coins minted per year drops sharply after each halving, from over three million in 2010 to about 165,000 in 2025 (Blockchain.com, 2026).
nodes.definition: Bitcoins minted each year, dropping in steps at each halving.

nodes.label: Halving era
nodes.body: The subsidy started at 50 bitcoin and halves every 210,000 blocks; the fourth halving, on 2024-04-20, set it at 3.125 bitcoin (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026).
nodes.definition: The subsidy halves every 210,000 blocks; the fourth halving, on 2024-04-20, set it at 3.125 bitcoin.

nodes.label: Mining
nodes.body: The third part, Mining capacity, shows the computing power securing the chain, which is chapter 2's security by computation made visible (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Hash power
nodes.body: Hash power is the total rate of guesses miners make in the proof-of-work search (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Network hash rate
nodes.body: The chart Network hash rate, EH/s plots the estimate in exahashes per second - a billion billion hashes each second - on a logarithmic scale (Blockchain.com, 2026).
nodes.example: hashes per second securing the chain
nodes.definition: The estimated number of hashes the whole network computes per second, in exahashes (10^18) per second.

nodes.label: Annual hash rate
nodes.body: Average hash rate by year shows it rising from about 4.358e-12 EH/s in 2009 to 952.8 EH/s in 2026, a factor of about 2.19e14 - the dashboard's 'about 200 trillion times' (Blockchain.com, 2026).
nodes.definition: The hash rate averaged over each year, on a logarithmic axis because it spans about fourteen orders of magnitude.

nodes.label: Relationship
nodes.body: Setting price against hash rate asks whether security followed value (Blockchain.com, 2026).

nodes.label: Price vs hash rate
nodes.body: The Price vs hash rate scatter puts price against hash rate on logarithmic scales, coloured from early to recent, so the joint rise of both shows as a path to the upper right (Blockchain.com, 2026).
nodes.example: price against hash rate over time
nodes.definition: A scatter of price against hash rate, both on logarithmic scales, coloured from early to recent.

nodes.label: Provenance
nodes.body: Every chart rests on one data source, and its limits belong on the page (Blockchain.com, 2026).

nodes.label: Data source
nodes.body: The dashboard states where its numbers come from and how current they are (Blockchain.com, 2026).

nodes.label: Blockchain.com snapshot
nodes.body: The data are a snapshot of Blockchain.com's public charts, sampled about every four days and taken when the page was built - so the numbers change only when the page is rebuilt (Blockchain.com, 2026).
nodes.definition: A snapshot of Blockchain.com's public charts taken when the page was built - not a live feed.

nodes.label: Hash-rate estimate
nodes.body: Hash rate is an estimate derived from difficulty and block times, because no one can count every miner's hashes directly (Blockchain.com, 2026).
nodes.definition: The hash rate cannot be observed directly; it is estimated from mining difficulty and block times.

findings: The dashboard shows seventeen years of Bitcoin in three parts - price, minted coins and mining capacity - drawn from Blockchain.com's public charts and sampled about every four days, as a snapshot rather than a live feed.

The dashboard's statements recompute from its own data: 20,087,925 bitcoins in circulation is 95.66 per cent of the 21 million cap; yearly average hash rate grew from 4.358e-12 EH/s in 2009 to 952.8 EH/s in 2026, a factor of about 2.19e14, matching its 'about 200 trillion times'; and the fourth halving on 2024-04-20 set the subsidy at 3.125 bitcoin, as the Bitcoin Wiki records.

For the course, the dashboard makes chapters 1 and 2 visible: the supply schedule and halvings of chapter 1 as a stepped curve and shrinking yearly issuance, and chapter 2's security by computation as a hash rate spanning fourteen orders of magnitude.

The snapshot was spot-checked against the Blockchain.com API on 2026-09-25: the market price and the hash rate match exactly at shared dates, for example 78521.7 dollars on 2026-08-26 and 825.5 EH/s on 2026-08-28.
